blocks.text: Attention is the mechanism that lets a model decide, for every token it is processing, which other tokens in the sequence actually matter for understanding this one, rather than treating every word as equally relevant.

It is the core building block behind every transformer based model discussed throughout this course, and understanding it at a working level makes later topics on model architecture, context windows, and fine-tuning behavior far easier to follow.
1. The Problem Attention Solves

blocks.alt: Treating all tokens equally is compared against attention, which lets some tokens matter more

blocks.text: Consider the sentence, the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too small. Understanding what it refers to, the trophy or the suitcase, requires focusing on specific earlier words, not treating every word in the sentence as equally important.
Attention gives a model a learned way to do exactly this, dynamically deciding how much weight to give each other token when building the representation of the current one.
2. Query, Key, and Value, The Core Idea

blocks.alt: A query and a key combine to produce an attention score

blocks.text: Attention works using three learned projections of each token, a query, a key, and a value. The query represents what the current token is looking for, the key represents what each other token has to offer, and comparing a query against every key produces a score for how relevant that other token is.

This query, key, value pattern is not unique to transformers, it is the same basic idea behind a search engine, a query is compared against many keys, and the best matching results, values, are returned.
3. Computing Attention Scores

For a given token query, its score against every other token key is computed, typically through a dot product, a mathematical operation that produces a higher number when two vectors point in a similar direction, meaning they are more related.
This produces a raw score for every pair of positions in the sequence, how much position one should attend to position two, position three, and so on.
4. Turning Scores Into Weights With Softmax

blocks.alt: Raw scores pass through softmax to become attention weights

blocks.text: Raw attention scores are converted into weights that sum to one using a function called softmax, which turns the highest scores into the largest weights while keeping every weight positive.
These weights are what get applied to the tokens that matter most, a token relevant to the current one ends up with a large weight, while an irrelevant token ends up with a weight close to zero.
5. Weighting the Values to Produce the Output

blocks.alt: A value combines with a weighted sum to produce the output representation

blocks.text: Once the attention weights are computed, they are used to combine the value vectors of every token into a single weighted sum, producing the output representation for the current token, one shaped heavily by whichever tokens received the highest attention weight.

code.content:
# A simplified single-head attention computation
scores = query @ key.transpose()
weights = softmax(scores / sqrt(key_dimension))
output = weights @ value

blocks.text: 6. Multi-Head Attention, Several Views at Once

blocks.alt: Several attention heads combine into one combined view

blocks.text: Rather than computing attention just once, transformer models run several attention computations in parallel, called heads, each with its own learned query, key, and value projections, then combine their outputs together.

This lets the model capture several different kinds of relationships at once, one head might focus on grammatical structure while another focuses on topic relevance, and combining them produces a richer overall representation than a single attention computation could.

blocks.title: Multi-head, not multiple separate models
blocks.content: The different attention heads are part of the same layer, trained together, not separate models, they simply learn to specialize in different kinds of relationships during training.

blocks.text: 7. Self-Attention vs Cross-Attention

blocks.alt: Self-attention within the same sequence is compared against cross-attention between two sequences

blocks.text: When every query, key, and value comes from the same sequence, comparing tokens within one input to each other, this is called self-attention, and it is what powers most modern decoder only language models covered in this course.

Cross-attention instead compares queries from one sequence against keys and values from a different sequence, historically used in encoder-decoder architectures where a decoder attends to an encoder representation of a separate input.

blocks.text: 8. Why Attention Matters for Fine-Tuning

Understanding attention matters practically for fine-tuning because several efficient fine-tuning methods covered later in this course, LoRA in particular, insert their trainable parameters directly into the attention layers, since that is where much of a model expressive capacity lives.
A basic grasp of how attention works makes it far easier to understand why those methods target the layers they do, rather than treating them as an unexplained implementation detail.
9. Attention and Long Context

blocks.alt: A longer input requires more attention comparisons, raising compute cost

blocks.text: Attention compares every token against every other token, which means the amount of computation grows quickly as the input sequence gets longer, a cost that becomes a real practical constraint for very long documents or conversations.

This growing cost is a major reason context window limits exist and why techniques for handling long context efficiently remain an active area of ongoing research, a topic that resurfaces later in this course when discussing training infrastructure.
Worked Example
Given the sentence, the engineer fixed the bug because she found the root cause quickly, a model processing the word she needs to figure out which earlier word it refers to.

Through attention, when computing the representation for she, the query for that position ends up producing a high score against the key for engineer, since the two are related, and a much lower score against unrelated words like bug or quickly, so the resulting representation for she is shaped heavily by its connection to engineer.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating attention as a black box rather than understanding it as a learned weighting mechanism over query, key, and value comparisons
Confusing self-attention, within one sequence, with cross-attention, between two different sequences
Assuming multi-head attention runs several separate models, when it runs several parallel projections within the same layer
Ignoring how attention cost grows with sequence length when reasoning about context window and infrastructure limits

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a sentence with a pronoun that refers back to an earlier noun. Walk through, in your own words, which earlier token you would expect the attention mechanism to weight most heavily when processing that pronoun, and why.
Key Takeaway

Attention lets a model dynamically decide which other tokens matter most for understanding the current one, computed through query, key, and value comparisons and combined across multiple heads, and it is the core mechanism that both powers transformer models and shapes where efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA choose to insert their trainable parameters.
